Casablanca Records released it as the album's second single on June 23, 1979. The song was produced by Summer's regular collaborators Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte, and co-written by Summer and the members of Brooklyn Dreams, Bruce Sudano, Joe "Bean" Esposito and Edward "Eddie" Hokenson. "Bad Girls" was a massive success, peaking within the Top 10 of the charts in seven countries, including New Zealand and Spain. In the United States, it spent five weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100, from the weeks of July 14 to August 11, 1979, and sold over two million copies, simultaneously becoming, alongside "Hot Stuff", her most successful single. It helped the Bad Girls album to reach multi-platinum status in the United States.

sections.heading: Background and recording
sections.wikitext:
The inspiration for Summer to write "Bad Girls" came after one of her assistants was offended by a [[police officer]] who thought she was a [[Sex worker|prostitute]]. A rough version of the song had originally been written a couple of years before its release. [[Casablanca Records]]' founder [[Neil Bogart]], upon hearing it, wanted Summer to give it to [[Cher]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Ordinary Girl: The Journey |last=Summer |first=Donna |author-link=Donna Summer |author2=Marc Eliot |year=2003 |publisher=Villard |location=New York |isbn=1400060311 |page=[https://archive.org/details/ordinarygirl00donn/page/172 172] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/ordinarygirl00donn/page/172 }}</ref> Summer refused and put it away for a couple of years.

A [[Twelve-inch single|12-inch]] version of "Bad Girls" was released as a [[Medley (music)|medley]] with "[[Hot Stuff (Donna Summer song)|Hot Stuff]]". Although "Hot Stuff" was extended for the release, "Bad Girls" remained in the original full-length album version. A [[Demo (music)|demo]] version of "Bad Girls" was released on the [[Special edition|deluxe edition]] of the ''[[Bad Girls (Donna Summer album)|Bad Girls]]'' album.
sections.text:
The inspiration for Summer to write "Bad Girls" came after one of her assistants was offended by a police officer who thought she was a prostitute. A rough version of the song had originally been written a couple of years before its release. Casablanca Records' founder Neil Bogart, upon hearing it, wanted Summer to give it to Cher. Summer refused and put it away for a couple of years.

A 12-inch version of "Bad Girls" was released as a medley with "Hot Stuff". Although "Hot Stuff" was extended for the release, "Bad Girls" remained in the original full-length album version. A demo version of "Bad Girls" was released on the deluxe edition of the Bad Girls album.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext: ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine called "Bad Girls" a "brassy [[disco]] track, which features party sounding production embellishments like hems and whistles."<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Billboard|date=May 26, 1979|accessdate=2023-03-27|page=87|title=Top Single Picks|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_iQEAAAAMBAJ}}</ref> ''[[Record World]]'' magazine said that Summer's "sultry reading is perfect for the threatening street theme."<ref name=rw>{{cite magazine|magazine=Record World|date=May 26, 1979|accessdate=2023-02-11|title=Hits of the Week|page=1|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/70s/79/RW-1979-05-26.pdf}}</ref>
sections.text: Billboard magazine called "Bad Girls" a "brassy disco track, which features party sounding production embellishments like hems and whistles." Record World magazine said that Summer's "sultry reading is perfect for the threatening street theme."

sections.heading: Commercial performance
sections.wikitext:
For the week of June 23, 1979, Summer made history as the first female artist to send multiple songs to the top ten on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 as "Bad Girls" vaulted up from number 11 to number 5 that week all while Summer's "Hot Stuff" remained number one.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/70s/1979/Billboard%201979-06-23.pdf |title=Billboard Hot 100 Chart Bound - For week ending June 23, 1979 |magazine=Billboard |date=June 23, 1979 |page=72 |accessdate=March 23, 2025}}</ref>

Eventually, "Bad Girls" reached the top of the Hot 100 for the week of July 14, 1979, where it would stay for five weeks outperforming "Hot Stuff", which had topped the chart for three weeks.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/70s/1979/Billboard%201979-07-14.pdf |title=Billboard Hot 100 Chart Bound - For week ending July 14, 1979 |magazine=Billboard |page=94 |date=July 14, 1979 |accessdate=March 23, 2025}}</ref>
sections.text:
For the week of June 23, 1979, Summer made history as the first female artist to send multiple songs to the top ten on the Billboard Hot 100 as "Bad Girls" vaulted up from number 11 to number 5 that week all while Summer's "Hot Stuff" remained number one.

Eventually, "Bad Girls" reached the top of the Hot 100 for the week of July 14, 1979, where it would stay for five weeks outperforming "Hot Stuff", which had topped the chart for three weeks.

sections.heading: Awards and nominations
sections.wikitext: "Bad Girls" was nominated for Favorite Pop/Rock Single, and won for Favorite Pop/Rock Female Artist, at the [[American Music Awards of 1980]]. Summer was also nominated for the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for [[Grammy Award for Best Disco Recording|Best Disco Recording]] at the [[22nd Annual Grammy Awards]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.grammy.com/artists/donna-summer/14046|title=Donna Summer|website=[[Grammy Awards]]|access-date=7 March 2023}}</ref>
sections.text: "Bad Girls" was nominated for Favorite Pop/Rock Single, and won for Favorite Pop/Rock Female Artist, at the American Music Awards of 1980. Summer was also nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Disco Recording at the 22nd Annual Grammy Awards.
